chapter.name: Water Resources
chapter.blurb: Water is renewable through the hydrological cycle, yet scarcity is caused mainly by over-exploitation, unequal access and pollution rather than low rainfall alone. India has built hydraulic structures since ancient times; modern multi-purpose dams like Bhakra-Nangal, Hirakud and Sardar Sarovar integrate irrigation, power, water supply and flood control, but draw real criticism for their ecological and social costs and have triggered inter-state disputes such as the one over Koyna. Traditional, region-specific rainwater harvesting -- guls/kuls, inundation channels, khadins/johads and Rajasthan's rooftop-fed tankas -- offers a different path, one still being revived today, from Tamil Nadu's compulsory law to Gendathur's village-wide adoption and Meghalaya's centuries-old bamboo drip irrigation.

scope_in.item: Explain why water is a renewable resource via the hydrological cycle, and state that water scarcity is caused mainly by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access rather than by low rainfall alone
Describe how population growth and the expansion of irrigated, dry-season agriculture add to water scarcity
Describe how industrialisation and urbanisation, including unregulated groundwater pumping by housing societies, add to water scarcity
Explain how bad water quality, caused by domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers, can itself cause water scarcity even where water is plentiful
State the goal and service-level target of the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM), and that the Atal Bhujal Yojana (Atal Jal) targets water-stressed Gram Panchayats

Describe ancient India's hydraulic structures named in the chapter: Sringaverapura, the era of Chandragupta Maurya, Kalinga/Nagarjunakonda/Bennur/Kolhapur, Bhopal Lake, and the Hauz Khas tank built by Allauddin Khilji

State the chapter's definition of a dam, that the word 'dam' refers to the reservoir rather than the structure, and its classification by structure (timber/embankment/masonry) and by height (large/major, or low/medium/high)

List the functions of a modern multi-purpose dam (irrigation, electricity generation, water supply, flood control, recreation, inland navigation, fish breeding) and explain why Nehru called dams the 'temples of modern India'

Describe the Bhakra-Nangal project (Sutluj-Beas basin) and the Hirakud project (Mahanadi basin) as the chapter's named examples of multi-purpose projects, including their location on the chapter's map 'India: Major Rivers and Dams'

List the ecological and social criticisms of multi-purpose projects and large dams: effect on river flow and sedimentation, river fragmentation and migration, floodplain submergence, flood-triggering and flood-control failure, soil erosion and silt loss, induced earthquakes and water-borne disease, and cropping-pattern change leading to salinisation
State the aims of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana, including its 'har khet ko pani' and 'per drop more crop' slogans

Describe the Sardar Sarovar project on the Narmada River: the four states it covers, and the area/village/district figures given for Gujarat plus the areas covered in Rajasthan and Maharashtra, including its location on the chapter's map
Describe the Krishna-Godavari dispute involving Maharashtra's diversion of water at Koyna and the states objecting to it

Explain why water harvesting was seen as an alternative to multi-purpose projects, and describe region-specific traditional techniques: guls/kuls (Western Himalayas), inundation channels (Bengal flood plains), and khadins/johads (Jaisalmer/other parts of Rajasthan)

Describe the traditional tanka system of Rajasthan (Bikaner, Phalodi, Barmer): its construction, connection to rooftops, the discarded first rainfall, storage till the next rainfall, palar pani, and the Phalodi size example

Describe Tamil Nadu's compulsory rooftop rainwater harvesting law
Describe the Shillong/Meghalaya contrast between nearby record rainfall and local water shortage, and the household water-share figure given for rooftop harvesting

Describe the Gendathur (Mysuru, Karnataka) rooftop rainwater harvesting case study and its stated figures: number of households, annual precipitation, collection efficiency, number of fillings, litres collected per house, and the net litres figure stated for the village
Describe the bamboo drip irrigation system of Meghalaya: the age of the system, the litres entering it, and the drops per minute delivered to the plant

concepts.name: Water: a renewable resource and the causes of water scarcity
concepts.description: Water renews through the hydrological cycle, but scarcity is mostly caused by over-exploitation, unequal access and pollution rather than low rainfall alone; JJM and Atal Bhujal Yojana are the chapter's named government responses.
concepts.idea: Water is a renewable resource because it moves continuously through the hydrological cycle, but scarcity still occurs because of over-exploitation, unequal access and pollution, not merely low rainfall.
concepts.rule: Freshwater is renewed and recharged through the hydrological cycle, which makes water a renewable resource. Water scarcity is not caused only by low rainfall or drought-prone regions; in most cases it is caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access to water among different social groups, driven by a growing population's need for food and water, over-exploitation of water for dry-season irrigation, and industrialisation and urbanisation (including unregulated groundwater pumping by housing societies). An area can have ample water and still face scarcity if that water is polluted by domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers. The Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) aims to give every rural household piped water at a service level of 55 litres per capita per day. The Atal Bhujal Yojana (Atal Jal) targets water-stressed Gram Panchayats.
concepts.example: A city can have plentiful water in its reservoirs and still suffer scarcity if that water is polluted by industrial waste -- scarcity caused by quality, not quantity.

questions.a: District Y is more likely to report water scarcity. Its factories discharging waste freely will pollute the water with domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals and other pollutants, making it hazardous for use even if quantity is sufficient. Its rapidly growing population increases demand for domestic use and food, encouraging over-exploitation of water for irrigation. Its many private borewells mean unregulated groundwater pumping, which the chapter links to falling groundwater levels and depletion. District X controls pollution and does not show the same population and groundwater pressures, so it is less likely to face scarcity from these causes even with similar rainfall.

concepts.name: Dams and multi-purpose river projects: history, definition and functions
concepts.description: India has built hydraulic structures since ancient times; a modern dam is a barrier creating a reservoir and is now built for many integrated purposes, classified by structure and by height.
concepts.idea: Dams have been built in India since ancient times to conserve and manage water; a modern dam is a barrier that creates a reservoir and is now built for many integrated purposes, not irrigation alone.
concepts.rule: Archaeological records show India building hydraulic structures since ancient times: a sophisticated water harvesting system at Sringaverapura (near Allahabad) channelling Ganga flood water in the 1st century B.C.; extensive dams, lakes and irrigation systems under Chandragupta Maurya; irrigation works at Kalinga (Odisha), Nagarjunakonda (Andhra Pradesh), Bennur (Karnataka) and Kolhapur (Maharashtra); Bhopal Lake, one of the largest artificial lakes of its time, in the 11th century; and the Hauz Khas tank in Delhi, built by Allauddin Khilji in the 13th-14th century to supply the Siri Fort area. A dam is a barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir, lake or impoundment; the word 'dam' refers to the reservoir rather than the structure. Most dams have a spillway or weir for water to flow through. Dams are classified by structure (timber, embankment or masonry dams) or by height (large and major dams, or low, medium height and high dams). Modern dams are multi-purpose projects, built for irrigation, electricity generation, water supply for domestic and industrial use, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding. Jawaharlal Nehru called dams the 'temples of modern India' because they would integrate the development of agriculture and the village economy with industrialisation and urban growth. In the Sutluj-Beas river basin, the Bhakra-Nangal project is used for both hydel power and irrigation; the Hirakud project in the Mahanadi basin integrates water conservation with flood control.
concepts.example: The Bhakra-Nangal project in the Sutluj-Beas basin shows how one dam can serve two purposes at once, hydel power production and irrigation.

concepts.name: Multi-purpose projects: criticisms and case studies
concepts.description: Multi-purpose projects and large dams bring real benefits but have also drawn serious ecological and social criticism, grounded here in the Sardar Sarovar project and the Krishna-Godavari (Koyna) dispute.
concepts.idea: Multi-purpose projects and large dams bring real benefits but have also drawn serious criticism for their ecological and social costs, which the chapter grounds in named case studies like Sardar Sarovar and the Krishna-Godavari dispute.
concepts.rule: Criticisms of multi-purpose projects and large dams listed in the chapter: they affect the natural flow of rivers, causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir, which results in rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for aquatic life; they fragment rivers, making migration difficult for aquatic fauna, especially for spawning; reservoirs on floodplains submerge existing vegetation and soil, which then decomposes; dams built to control floods have ironically triggered floods due to sedimentation, and big dams have mostly been unsuccessful in controlling floods during excessive rainfall; these floods devastate life, property and cause soil erosion; sedimentation deprives floodplains of silt, a natural fertiliser, adding to land degradation; multi-purpose projects have also been observed to induce earthquakes and cause water-borne diseases and pests; and irrigation has changed cropping patterns towards water-intensive and commercial crops, with ecological consequences like salinisation of the soil. The Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana aims to expand assured irrigation (har khet ko pani) and improve water-use efficiency (per drop more crop). The Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada River in Gujarat is one of India's largest water resource projects, covering four states (Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Rajasthan): it will irrigate 18.45 lakh hectare of land across 3112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat, plus 2,46,000 hectare in Barmer and Jalore (Rajasthan) and 37,500 hectare in tribal hilly Maharashtra (through lift); about 75 per cent of Gujarat's command area is drought-prone, and the entire command area in Rajasthan is drought-prone. The Krishna-Godavari dispute arises from Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh objecting to the Maharashtra government diverting more water at Koyna for a multi-purpose project, which would reduce downstream flow with adverse consequences for agriculture and industry in their states.
concepts.example: Sedimentation is both a criticism, since it fills reservoirs and worsens floods, and a downstream loss, since it deprives floodplains of the silt that used to fertilise them naturally.

concepts.name: Rainwater harvesting: traditional regional techniques
concepts.description: Faced with the problems of multi-purpose projects, many looked back to a long Indian tradition of region-specific rainwater harvesting techniques adapted to local ecological conditions.
concepts.idea: Given the disadvantages of multi-purpose projects, water harvesting was seen as a viable socio-economic and environmental alternative, drawing on a long Indian tradition of region-specific techniques.
concepts.rule: Ancient India had an extraordinary tradition of water harvesting, with techniques suited to local rainfall regimes, soil types and ecological conditions: diversion channels called guls or kuls in the hill and mountainous regions of the Western Himalayas, used for agriculture; rooftop rainwater harvesting, commonly practised to store drinking water, particularly in Rajasthan; inundation channels developed in the flood plains of Bengal to irrigate fields; and, in arid and semi-arid regions, agricultural fields converted into rain-fed storage structures that let water stand and moisten the soil, called khadins in Jaisalmer and johads in other parts of Rajasthan. Besides rainwater, these techniques harvested groundwater, river water and flood water.
concepts.example: A hill farmer in the Western Himalayas and a farmer in the flood plains of Bengal solve the same basic problem, getting water to fields, with two completely different traditional structures, a diversion channel (kul) and an inundation channel, because their ecological conditions differ.

concepts.name: Rooftop rainwater harvesting and Rajasthan's tankas
concepts.description: In Rajasthan's dry regions, households built underground tankas fed by rooftop rain, a self-contained system for storing the purest drinking water through the dry season, now in decline where canal water is available.
concepts.idea: In Rajasthan's dry regions, households built underground tankas fed by rooftop rain, a self-contained system for storing the purest drinking water through the long dry season, though it is now in decline where canal water has become available.
concepts.rule: In the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan, particularly Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, almost all houses traditionally had underground tanks or tankas for storing drinking water. Tanks could be as large as a big room; one household in Phalodi had a tank 6.1 metres deep, 4.27 metres long and 2.44 metres wide. Tankas were part of a well-developed rooftop rainwater harvesting system, built inside the main house or courtyard, and connected to the sloping roofs by a pipe; the first spell of rain was not collected, since it would clean the roofs and pipes, and only the rainwater from subsequent showers was collected. Rainwater could be stored in tankas till the next rainfall, making it an extremely reliable source of drinking water in summers when other sources dried up. This rainwater, called palar pani, is considered the purest form of natural water; many houses built underground rooms adjoining the tanka to keep cool in summer. Today, in western Rajasthan, the practice is on the decline because of the perennial Indira Gandhi Canal, though some households still keep their tankas because they do not like the taste of tap water.
concepts.example: A household in Phalodi with a tank 6.1 metres deep shows that a tanka was not a small pot but a room-sized underground structure built to carry a family through the whole dry season on stored rain.

concepts.name: Modern revival and local case studies: Tamil Nadu, Shillong, Gendathur and bamboo drip irrigation
concepts.description: Rooftop rainwater harvesting has been revived and adapted in very different modern settings, from a state-wide law in Tamil Nadu to a single celebrated village in Karnataka and a centuries-old bamboo system in Meghalaya.
concepts.idea: Rooftop rainwater harvesting has been revived and adapted in very different modern settings across India, from a state-wide law in Tamil Nadu to a single celebrated village in Karnataka and a centuries-old bamboo system in Meghalaya.
concepts.rule: Tamil Nadu is the first state in India to make rooftop rainwater harvesting structures compulsory for all houses across the state, with legal provisions to punish defaulters. In Shillong, Meghalaya, rooftop rainwater harvesting is the most common practice; although Cherapunjee and Mawsynram, just 55 km from Shillong, receive the highest rainfall in the world, Shillong itself faces acute water shortage, and rooftop harvesting supplies nearly 15-25 per cent of a household's total water requirement. In Gendathur, a remote village in Mysuru, Karnataka, nearly 200 households have installed rooftop rainwater harvesting, earning the village a reputation for being rich in rainwater; Gendathur receives an annual precipitation of 1,000 mm, and with 80 per cent collection efficiency and about 10 fillings, every house can collect and use about 50,000 litres of water annually, with the chapter stating that the net amount of rainwater harvested annually from the 200 houses amounts to 1,00,000 litres. In Meghalaya, a 200-year-old bamboo drip irrigation system taps stream and spring water: about 18-20 litres of water enters the bamboo pipe system, is transported over hundreds of metres, and is reduced to 20-80 drops per minute at the site of the plant, with pipes taken high above the ground where they cross a road.
concepts.example: The same basic idea, rooftop rainwater harvesting, looks completely different in Tamil Nadu (a state law), Shillong (high regional rainfall alongside local scarcity) and Gendathur (a single well-documented village), showing how one technique gets adapted to very different local situations.
